claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn initially has a metastable FCC single-crystal structure.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal may contain local chemical short-range-order clusters.
Shockley partial dislocations create intrinsic stacking faults during deformation.
Local chemical short-range-order clusters lower the stacking-fault energy.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a bulk FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
Chemical short-range order stabilizes the HCP-like intrinsic stacking faults.
At cryogenic temperatures, stacking-fault energy decreases and may become negative or near zero.
Low or negative stacking-fault energy favors stacking faults over full-dislocation glide.
The <11-1> orientation maximizes resolved shear stress on a {111} slip plane.
Shockley partial nucleation in the <11-1> orientation requires a higher applied stress than in the <110> orientation.
Short-range-order clusters prevent the cooperative atomic rearrangement required for a true FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
The yield stress in the <11-1> orientation will be approximately 15-20% higher than in the <110> orientation.
Post-yield material will contain a high density of intrinsic stacking faults with local HCP-like stacking.
Diffraction or pair-distribution-function measurements will show no distinct HCP phase peaks and only stacking-fault-related broadening of FCC peaks.
The HCP-like regions will be confined to one or two atomic layers rather than forming coherent HCP domains.
FCC-to-HCP transformation can unlock or annihilate Lomer-Cottrell locks and thereby facilitate dislocation motion.
The proposed regime is one in which dislocation nucleation dominates over twinning and phase transformation.
Distinct sharp HCP diffraction peaks or coherent HCP domains thicker than 5-10 atomic layers would falsify the stacking-fault-only interpretation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes higher <11-1> yield stress to a higher critical resolved shear stress, while the mechanism says this orientation maximizes resolved shear stress. For a fixed material CRSS, maximizing the Schmid factor would normally reduce, not increase, the required applied tensile stress; no orientation-dependent CRSS evidence is supplied to resolve this.
